components.detail: Germany; Mosel, Rheingau and Pfalz for estate-grown Winzersekt

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Mostly tank method; Winzersekt uses bottle fermentation from estate fruit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Basic Sekt released quickly; Winzersekt rests months on its lees

composition.process: The best examples take Riesling's racy acidity through a bottle fermentation, giving orchard fruit real backbone.

name: Albariño
description: A saline, citrusy coastal dweller from Spain's rainy northwest, seemingly engineered by nature to accompany shellfish. Often carries a whisper of sea spray.
funFact: Across the border in Portugal the same grape is called Alvarinho, where it stars in the finest bottlings of Vinho Verde.

serve.how: Chill it down, pour a modest measure into a white wine glass, and let it warm slightly in the glass rather than over-icing the bottle. Give it a quick swirl and look for the whisper of sea spray behind the lemon zest and white peach. It is at its absolute best alongside shellfish — drink it the way they do in Galicia, with something briny on the table.

composition.summary: Albariño from the rainy Atlantic coast of Rías Baixas in Galicia.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Albariño; the same grape as Portugal's Alvarinho across the Minho

components.label: Region
components.detail: Rías Baixas, Galicia, especially Val do Salnés on granite

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool stainless fermentation; some producers age on fine lees

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rarely oaked; most is bottled young and drunk younger

composition.process: Cool fermentation in steel preserves the thick-skinned grape's citrus aromatics and that whisper of Atlantic salt.

name: Assyrtiko
description: A volcanic survivor from Santorini that keeps razor acidity even under scorching Aegean sun. Bone dry, smoky, and startlingly saline.
funFact: On windswept Santorini, Assyrtiko vines are woven into low basket shapes called kouloura, with the grapes growing inside for protection.

serve.how: Serve it a touch warmer than a simple summer white — too cold and you mute the smoke and beeswax that make it special. Pour, swirl, and take a moment with the nose: flint and salt first, then lemon underneath. Its razor acidity begs for food, so treat it like a serious dry white and drink it through a meal rather than before one.

composition.summary: Assyrtiko grown on Santorini's volcanic ash, on ungrafted, basket-trained vines.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Assyrtiko; vines ungrafted, phylloxera never survived the volcanic soil

components.label: Region
components.detail: Santorini, in the Aegean; also mainland Greek plantings

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fermented dry in steel; the barrel-aged version is called Nykteri

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly none; Nykteri and top cuvées see oak and time

composition.process: Vines woven into low kouloura baskets shelter the fruit from Aegean wind, so acidity survives ferocious sun.

name: Chablis
description: Chardonnay stripped to its skeleton: steely, saline, and rarely troubled by oak. It grows in cold northern Burgundy atop ancient seabed.
funFact: Chablis vines grow in Kimmeridgian limestone studded with fossilized oyster shells from a sea that covered the region 150 million years ago.

serve.how: Resist the ice bucket — over-chilled Chablis tastes like cold water, while at cellar-cool temperature the oyster-shell and flint notes come alive. Pour into a white wine glass, swirl gently, and let it sit ten minutes if it seems shy. Taste for the steely, saline finish; this is Chardonnay with its makeup off, and premier cru bottles reward slow, attentive sipping.
pair: sole or other delicate white fish

composition.summary: Pure Chardonnay grown on Kimmeridgian limestone in the cold north of Burgundy.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay only, with no other variety permitted

components.label: Region
components.detail: Chablis, northern Burgundy, on fossil-studded Kimmeridgian limestone

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Steel or neutral wood; oak is deliberately kept off the fruit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Village wines see steel; Grand Crus may rest in old barrels

composition.process: Refusing new oak leaves nothing between you and the cold-climate acidity and oyster-shell minerality of the site.

name: Chardonnay
description: The great shape-shifter of white grapes, appearing lean and steely in cool cellars yet golden and buttery wherever oak barrels lurk. Found on virtually every wine list on Earth.
funFact: DNA analysis at UC Davis revealed Chardonnay is a natural cross between noble Pinot Noir and the humble medieval grape Gouais Blanc.

serve.temp: 48-55°F — cooler for unoaked, warmer for oaked
serve.how: Match the chill to the style: lean, unoaked bottles want a proper fridge chill, while rich, barrel-aged versions show best only lightly cooled so the butter and vanilla can unfurl. Pour into a generous white wine glass and swirl well — oaked Chardonnay especially rewards aeration. Notice whether you get green apple and citrus (steel) or toast and vanilla (oak); it's the same grape playing two different characters.

composition.summary: Chardonnay, a Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc cross, born in Burgundy and grown everywhere.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay; a natural cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc

components.label: Region
components.detail: Côte de Beaune and Mâconnais in Burgundy; now every wine country

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Barrel fermentation, lees stirring and malolactic build the buttery style

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Anywhere from steel-only to a year in new French oak

composition.process: Malolactic fermentation generates diacetyl — the same compound in butter — which is where the 'buttery' Chardonnay comes from.

name: Chenin Blanc
description: The Loire's do-everything grape, capable of dry, sweet, still, and sparkling forms without breaking a sweat. Its searing acidity lets great examples age for half a century.
funFact: South Africa grows more Chenin Blanc than France does, where the grape has long gone by the local name 'Steen'.

serve.how: Check the style before you pour — Chenin runs from bone dry to honeyed, and drier versions take more chill than sweeter ones. Serve in a white wine glass, swirl, and hunt for the grape's odd, wonderful signature: quince and honey with a lanolin, wet-wool undertone. Its searing acidity keeps even off-dry bottles fresh, so if you own an aged Vouvray, give it a few minutes of air and sip patiently.

composition.summary: Chenin Blanc from the middle Loire, made dry, sweet, still or sparkling.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chenin Blanc; known as Steen across South Africa

components.label: Region
components.detail: Vouvray, Savennières, Montlouis and Anjou in the Loire Valley

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Sec to moelleux; botrytis for sweet, traditional method for sparkling

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Old barrels or steel; great examples last half a century

composition.process: Its extraordinary natural acidity lets a grower stop fermentation anywhere on the sugar scale and still make a balanced wine.

name: Gewürztraminer
description: An unmistakably perfumed specimen that smells of lychee and rose petals before you even lift the glass. Loud, golden, and impossible to confuse with anything else.
funFact: The grape takes its name from the village of Tramin in the Italian Alps, with 'Gewürz' meaning 'spice' in German.

serve.how: Don't over-chill it — this grape's whole point is perfume, and cold smothers it. Pour a smaller measure than usual into a white wine glass (it's rich and often high in alcohol), then smell before you sip: lychee and rose petal should leap out before the glass reaches your lips. On the palate, notice the oily, golden texture and ginger spice; it's a wine you sip, not gulp.

composition.summary: Gewürztraminer, a pink-skinned Traminer mutation named for the village of Tramin.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Gewürztraminer, an aromatic pink-skinned mutation of Traminer

components.label: Region
components.detail: Alsace above all; Alto Adige, Germany and New Zealand too

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Slow pressing of pink skins; often finished with a little sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; large neutral casks in Alsace, never new oak

composition.process: Its skins are loaded with terpenes — the same aromatic compounds in rose petals and lychee — which pressing coaxes out.

name: Grüner Veltliner
description: Austria's signature white, zippy and green-tinged with a telltale flick of white pepper on the finish. A sommelier favorite for its uncanny food friendliness.
funFact: Its peppery bite comes from rotundone, the same aroma compound found in actual black peppercorns and in Syrah.

serve.how: Serve it fridge-cool in a white wine glass — this is Austria's great table wine, built for drinking with food. Swirl and sniff for the telltale flick of white pepper over green apple and lime. It's famously the sommelier's escape hatch for hard-to-pair plates, so test it against vegetables that normally wreck wine, like asparagus or artichokes.

composition.summary: Grüner Veltliner from the terraced Danube valleys of Lower Austria.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Grüner Veltliner, Austria's most planted variety by a distance

components.label: Region
components.detail: Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal and the Weinviertel, in Lower Austria

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; oak is used sparingly if at all

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Fresh Steinfeder and Federspiel young; ripe Smaragd rewards years

composition.process: Clean steel fermentation preserves rotundone, the peppercorn compound that gives the wine its unmistakable green-pepper flick.

name: Muscadet
description: A briny, feather-light white from the Atlantic mouth of the Loire, made from the Melon de Bourgogne grape. It exists in near-perfect symbiosis with raw oysters.
funFact: Bottles labeled 'sur lie' rest on their spent yeast cells through the winter, picking up a subtle creaminess and a faint natural spritz.

serve.how: Chill it hard and pour it cold — Muscadet is a featherweight built for refreshment, not contemplation. Look for 'sur lie' on the label and notice the subtle creaminess and faint prickle it picks up from a winter resting on its yeast. The wine is almost neutral on its own; put a plate of raw oysters next to it and the briny, lemony pairing suddenly makes perfect sense.

composition.summary: Melon de Bourgogne from the Atlantic mouth of the Loire, aged on its lees.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Melon de Bourgogne, a Burgundian exile now unique to Nantes

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sèvre et Maine in the Pays Nantais, at the Loire's mouth

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fermented dry in tank or underground glass-lined vats

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 'Sur lie' bottlings rest on spent yeast through the winter

composition.process: Bottling straight off the lees without racking adds a creamy texture and faint prickle to an otherwise austere wine.

name: Picpoul de Pinet
description: A zesty Mediterranean white from the lagoons of the Languedoc, traditionally shipped in a distinctive tall green bottle. Built for oysters farmed within sight of its vines.
funFact: The grape's name, Piquepoul, translates roughly to 'lip stinger' — a nod to its bracing acidity.

serve.how: Serve it cold from the fridge in a white wine glass and don't overthink it — the tall green bottle is a promise of simple seaside pleasure. Take a sip and feel the 'lip-stinger' acidity that gives the grape its name, chased by lemon and a saline snap. It's the house pour of the Languedoc's oyster farms, so drink it with anything briny, fried, or fresh off the grill.

composition.summary: Piquepoul Blanc grown beside the oyster lagoons of the Languedoc coast.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Piquepoul Blanc; the name means roughly 'lip stinger'

components.label: Region
components.detail: Pinet and neighbouring villages beside the Étang de Thau, Languedoc

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked early and fermented cold to protect its bracing acidity

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; steel only, shipped in its tall green bottle

composition.process: Early picking in a hot Mediterranean region is the whole trick — it keeps the acid that oysters demand.

name: Pinot Grigio
description: A light, breezy sipper that evolved from a grayish-pink mutation of Pinot Noir. In its Italian form it is crisp and neutral; as Alsatian Pinot Gris it grows richer and spicier.
funFact: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the exact same grape — the 'gris' (gray) refers to the oddly grayish-blue tint of its skins.

serve.how: Chill it properly and pour into a white wine glass; Italian-style Pinot Grigio is about crisp refreshment, so drink it young and cold. Swirl lightly and look for pear, lemon, and a faint almond bitterness on the finish. If your bottle is a richer Alsatian Pinot Gris, serve it a few degrees warmer to let its spice and weight show.

composition.summary: Pinot Gris, a grey-skinned Pinot Noir mutation, crisp in Italy and richer in Alsace.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pinot Gris; a color mutation of Pinot Noir with greyish skins

components.label: Region
components.detail: Veneto, Friuli and Alto Adige in Italy; Alsace in France

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Pressed fast off pink skins in Italy; riper and fuller in Alsace

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None in the Italian style; Alsace bottlings can age well

composition.process: Quick pressing keeps the greyish-pink skins from tinting the juice, which is what makes the Italian style so pale.

name: Retsina
description: An ancient Greek oddity infused with pine resin during fermentation, giving it an unmistakable forest-floor perfume. Divisive, historic, and stubbornly still here.
funFact: The style descends from antiquity, when amphorae were sealed with pine resin and the flavor seeped into the wine — Greeks came to like it that way.

serve.glass: White wine glass (or small taverna tumbler)
serve.how: Serve it very cold — chill tames the pine and turns divisive into delicious. Pour small amounts into a white wine glass or, more authentically, a little taverna tumbler, and drink it with food rather than alone. Give the resin a chance: after a bite of something garlicky or briny, the forest-floor perfume clicks into place like it has for two thousand years.

composition.summary: Savatiano and Roditis from Attica, infused with Aleppo pine resin during fermentation.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Savatiano mainly, with Roditis and occasionally Assyrtiko

components.label: Region
components.detail: Attica and central Greece, around Athens

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Aleppo pine resin added to the must during fermentation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; the resin is racked off with the lees and bottled young

composition.process: Pine resin steeped in the fermenting must — a survival of amphora sealing — becomes the flavor rather than the container.

name: Riesling
description: A high-acid chameleon that ranges from bone dry to nectar sweet while somehow always tasting like itself. With age it develops a curious and prized whiff of petrol.
funFact: Riesling's first documented mention dates to 1435, in the cellar inventory of a German count at Rüsselsheim.

serve.how: Check the label first — Trocken means dry, Kabinett and Spätlese lean sweeter — and chill accordingly, with sweeter styles taking a colder serve. Pour into a white wine glass, swirl, and smell for lime and peach; in older bottles, hunt for that prized, curious whiff of petrol. The electric acidity means even off-dry Rieslings finish clean, which makes them the great secret weapon against spicy food.

composition.summary: Riesling from Germany's steep slate river slopes, made bone dry to nectar sweet.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Riesling, documented in Germany since 1435

components.label: Region
components.detail: Mosel slate, Rheingau, Pfalz and Nahe; also Alsace and Clare Valley

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fermentation halted where the grower wants it on the Prädikat scale

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Steel or large neutral Fuder casks; oak flavor is never welcome

composition.process: Stopping fermentation at a chosen point balances residual sugar against searing acidity, from trocken to lusciously sweet.

name: Sancerre
description: The most aristocratic form of Sauvignon Blanc, grown on flint and limestone hills overlooking the upper Loire. Smoky, precise, and perpetually in demand at wine bars.
funFact: Though famous for whites, the Sancerre appellation also covers reds and rosés made from Pinot Noir, a remnant of its pre-phylloxera past as red wine country.

serve.how: Serve it just cool, not cold — a few degrees warmer than everyday Sauvignon Blanc lets the smoky gunflint character surface over the grapefruit. Pour into a white wine glass, swirl, and take your time with the nose; the flint-and-chalk precision is what you paid for. Sip it alongside goat cheese and you'll taste one of the classic pairings in all of wine.
pair: crottin de Chavignol or any goat cheese

composition.summary: Sauvignon Blanc on the flint and limestone hills of the upper Loire.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sauvignon Blanc for the whites; Pinot Noir for its reds and rosés

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sancerre, upper Loire, on terres blanches, caillottes and silex

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; oak is used rarely and lightly

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Generally none; a few top cuvées see old barrels briefly

composition.process: Flint-rich silex soils and cold cellar fermentation give the smoky, gunflint edge that separates Sancerre from generic Sauvignon.

name: Sauvignon Blanc
description: A sharp, grassy creature that announces itself from across the room with a burst of gooseberry and cut grass. Thrives in the Loire, Marlborough, and refrigerators worldwide.
funFact: Its name derives from the French 'sauvage' (wild), and it is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon via a chance crossing with Cabernet Franc.

serve.how: Serve it cold from the fridge, poured into a white wine glass, and drink it young — freshness is the entire point. No swirling ceremony required: the gooseberry and cut-grass aromatics announce themselves from across the room. Notice how the zippy acidity cuts through herbs, greens, and tangy cheeses that flatten other wines.

composition.summary: Sauvignon Blanc, wild-named grape of the Loire, Bordeaux and New Zealand's Marlborough.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sauvignon Blanc; its name derives from 'sauvage', meaning wild

components.label: Region
components.detail: Loire Valley and Bordeaux in France; Marlborough in New Zealand

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool, protective fermentation preserves the thiols behind gooseberry and passionfruit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Steel and young; white Bordeaux blends see barrel fermentation

composition.process: Fermenting cold and away from oxygen protects volatile thiol compounds — the source of that shout of cut grass.

name: Sémillon
description: A quiet, waxy grape that plays two extremes: the backbone of golden Sauternes in Bordeaux, and a lean, ageless dry white in Australia's Hunter Valley.
funFact: Hunter Valley Sémillon is picked early at low alcohol and tastes almost neutral in youth, then miraculously develops honeyed, toasty depth over decades in bottle.

serve.how: Serve dry Sémillon just lightly chilled in a white wine glass so the waxy, lanolin texture isn't numbed away. Swirl and look past the quiet lemon for beeswax and, in aged Hunter Valley bottles, an astonishing honeyed-toast depth that appears with a little air. If yours is a sweet Sauternes-style bottling instead, chill it harder and pour small glasses for after dinner.
pair: flaky white fish in butter sauce

composition.summary: Sémillon, botrytis vessel in Bordeaux and a lean, ageless dry white in Australia.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sémillon; blended with Sauvignon Blanc in Bordeaux, solo in the Hunter

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sauternes and Graves in Bordeaux; the Hunter Valley, New South Wales

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Thin skins invite botrytis; the Hunter picks early at low alcohol

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sauternes in barriques; Hunter Sémillon unoaked, then decades in bottle

composition.process: In the Hunter it is picked barely ripe and never oaked, so all its complexity develops later in bottle.

name: Soave
description: A gentle Venetian white built on the Garganega grape, all pear and almond softened by volcanic soils. Once dismissed as cheap, its hillside crus are quietly excellent.
funFact: In the 1970s Soave was the best-selling imported Italian wine in the United States, outselling even Chianti.

serve.how: Chill it down and pour into a white wine glass; single-vineyard Classico bottles deserve a slightly warmer serve and a moment to open. Swirl and find the gentle pear and melon, then wait for the signature bitter-almond note on the finish — that's the Garganega grape's calling card. It's a soft-spoken wine, so pair it with delicate food that won't shout over it.

composition.summary: Garganega grown on volcanic hills east of Verona in the Veneto.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Garganega mainly, with Trebbiano di Soave or Chardonnay permitted

components.label: Region
components.detail: Soave and Soave Classico, on volcanic basalt hills near Verona

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; some producers rest it on fine lees

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Little to none; hillside crus and Riserva can take some wood

composition.process: Dark volcanic basalt on the Classico hills gives the salty, almond-skin bite that flatland Soave never manages.

name: Torrontés
description: Argentina's aromatic trickster: it smells sweet as a flower shop, then lands crisp and dry. Happiest in dizzyingly high desert vineyards.
funFact: Torrontés is a natural cross between Muscat of Alexandria and the Mission grape brought to the Americas by Spanish missionaries.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a white wine glass and enjoy the bait-and-switch: the nose promises a flower shop's worth of rose and muscat sweetness, then the palate lands crisp and dry. No decanting, no ceremony — just smell deeply before each sip to catch the perfume. It's built for aromatic, spiced food that matches its own volume.

composition.summary: Torrontés Riojano, an aromatic Argentine cross grown in high desert vineyards.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Torrontés Riojano; a Muscat of Alexandria × Criolla Chica cross

components.label: Region
components.detail: Cafayate in Salta, plus La Rioja and Mendoza, Argentina

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Pressed quickly off skins to keep bitterness out; fermented cold

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; steel and bottled young, with oak strictly avoided

composition.process: Fast pressing keeps its Muscat-derived terpenes aromatic without the phenolic bitterness those thick skins would otherwise contribute.

name: Txakoli
description: The Basque Country's electric, lightly fizzy white, low in alcohol and high in theatrics. Bartenders pour it from a great height to rouse its bubbles.
funFact: In San Sebastián's pintxo bars, Txakoli is traditionally poured from arm's length above the glass to aerate it and coax out its natural fizz.

serve.how: Chill it hard, then do it Basque-style: hold the bottle at arm's length above a flat tumbler and pour a long, thin stream to rouse the natural fizz — a few splashes on the counter are part of the ritual. Pour only a couple of inches at a time, so each pour is still cold and spritzy when you taste it. Notice the green apple, lime, and saline crackle; at barely 11% alcohol it's a light match for pintxos.

composition.summary: Hondarrabi Zuri from the Atlantic-lashed hills of the Basque Country.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Hondarrabi Zuri; the red Hondarrabi Beltza makes the rosé

components.label: Region
components.detail: Getariako, Bizkaiko and Arabako Txakolina, in Basque Spain

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked early at low ripeness; a light spritz retained at bottling

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; drunk within the year, ideally standing at a bar

composition.process: Early harvest in a cool, wet maritime climate keeps alcohol low and acidity high, with a faint prickle sealed in.

name: Vermentino
description: A sun-loving Mediterranean white with a pleasantly bitter, almond-skin farewell. It patrols the coasts of Sardinia, Liguria, and Corsica, where it moonlights as Rolle.
funFact: Vermentino di Gallura is the only DOCG, Italy's highest wine classification, on the entire island of Sardinia.

serve.how: Serve it fridge-cool in a white wine glass, ideally somewhere you can pretend there's a sea breeze. Swirl and taste for lime and green pear, then wait for the pleasantly bitter almond-skin farewell on the finish — that's the grape saying goodbye properly. It shines brightest with herb-flecked Mediterranean food and anything pulled from the sea.

composition.summary: Vermentino from Sardinia, Liguria and Corsica, where it also goes by Rolle.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Vermentino; Rolle in Provence, Pigato and Favorita in Italy

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sardinia's Gallura DOCG, plus Liguria, Tuscany, Corsica and Provence

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; brief skin contact adds texture and grip

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; a few producers age briefly on lees

composition.process: A short spell on the skins draws out the phenolics behind that gently bitter, almond-skin finish.

name: Vinho Verde
description: Portugal's 'green wine' — green as in young, not in color. Low in alcohol, lightly spritzy, and best consumed within sight of a beach.
funFact: The gentle fizz was originally an accident of secondary fermentation in bottle; today many producers add a small dose of carbon dioxide on purpose.

serve.how: This is the rare wine you genuinely cannot serve too cold — bury it in ice and pour it into a white wine glass beaded with condensation. Drink it young, within a year of the vintage, and feel the gentle prickle of spritz over lime and green apple. At around 10% alcohol it's an afternoon wine; no swirling or ceremony, just keep it cold.

composition.summary: Loureiro, Alvarinho and Arinto from the wet green northwest of Portugal.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Loureiro, Alvarinho, Arinto, Trajadura and Avesso, usually blended

components.label: Region
components.detail: Minho, between the Douro and the Spanish border, Portugal

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked early for low alcohol; a dose of CO2 supplies the fizz

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; the whole style is built on youth and freshness

composition.process: The spritz began as accidental bottle refermentation and is now added deliberately, keeping a lean wine lively.

name: Viognier
description: A lush, apricot-scented rarity rescued from the brink of extinction. Full-bodied and heady, it walks the line between opulence and excess.
funFact: By the 1960s Viognier had dwindled to roughly a dozen acres in Condrieu before a global revival brought it back from near extinction.

serve.how: Serve it warmer than most whites — too much chill locks away the apricot-and-honeysuckle perfume that is Viognier's whole reason for being. Pour into a generous white wine glass, swirl slowly, and give it ten minutes; the nose blooms as it warms. Notice the lush, almost oily texture and keep pours modest, since its heady richness and higher alcohol walk the line between opulence and excess.

composition.summary: Viognier from Condrieu and Château-Grillet in the northern Rhône, rescued from near-extinction.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Viognier; reduced to roughly a dozen acres by the 1960s

components.label: Region
components.detail: Condrieu and Château-Grillet in the northern Rhône; now worldwide

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked very ripe for apricot terpenes; often barrel-fermented with lees stirring

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Neutral oak for a few months; malolactic softens the acidity

composition.process: It must be picked at full ripeness for its apricot perfume to appear, which is why the alcohol runs high.

name: White Blend
description: A white sold by its blend rather than one grape: an aromatic variety such as Riesling, Viognier or Muscat for perfume, Chardonnay for body, Sauvignon Blanc or Pinot Grigio for snap. The American ones are often softly off-dry.
funFact: Alsace, which labels nearly all its wines by grape, keeps a name for its white blends: Edelzwicker, usually translated 'noble blend', which may mix the region's white varieties in any proportion.

serve.how: Chill it well but not ice-cold; under about 45°F the perfume of the aromatic grapes shuts down. A standard white wine glass suits it. Look for stone fruit and blossom first, then the rounder Chardonnay middle and a fresh finish; any sweetness shows as a soft, honeyed edge.

composition.summary: Two or more white grapes in any share, sold under a brand rather than a grape's name.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Any whites: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Viognier, Riesling, Pinot Grigio and Muscat among them

components.label: Region
components.detail: Made wherever white grapes grow, from Alsace and Bordeaux to California

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Pressed off the skins and fermented cool, each grape apart, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly steel, sometimes a touch of oak for the Chardonnay

composition.process: Blending lets a winemaker set perfume against body and acidity in proportions no single grape would give.
